introduction:
Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) has emerged as one of the most pressing global public health threats of the 21st century (1). The primary drivers of AMR are the overuse and misuse of antibiotics (2,3). Despite significant efforts by scientists in recent years to combat AMR, there is no sign of the trend slowing down. The emergence of resistant strains has led to a decline in the effectiveness of traditional antimicrobial drugs, an increase in treatment failure rates and a heightened risk of infection transmission, exacerbating individual morbidity and mortality risks while intensifying the public health burden (4–6). Research estimates that over 1.2 million direct deaths were attributable to antibiotic resistance in 2019. Without effective measures to curb antibiotic resistance, annual deaths are projected to rise to approximately 10 million by 2050 (7–9). The widespread use of antibiotics and other antimicrobial drugs during the COVID-19 pandemic has further exacerbated the spread of resistant strains (10–12). In the post-pandemic era, with the resumption of global travel and trade, the accelerated spread of resistant microorganisms, particularly in regions with limited healthcare resources and rampant antibiotic misuse, poses cross-border health risks. Consequently, addressing AMR has become even more urgent in the post-pandemic context. However, despite the growing severity of AMR, the development of new antibiotics has faced significant challenges due to high costs and low economic returns, leaving existing drugs increasingly inadequate against resistance threats. Antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) have gained widespread attention as an emerging antimicrobial strategy (13). AMPs, typically composed of 10-100 amino acids and integral to the immune system, are less likely to induce microbial resistance due to their unique mechanisms of action (14). Compared to traditional antibiotics, AMPs exhibit broad-spectrum antimicrobial activity, including antibacterial, antifungal, antiviral and anticancer properties (15). AMPs not only effectively combat resistant pathogens but also show significant potential in countering emerging viral infections like COVID-19 (16,17). Thus, the potential of AMPs as alternatives to antimicrobial drugs is particularly prominent in the post-pandemic era.
However, the diversity, wide origins, and multifunctionality of AMPs present substantial challenges in data management and information integration for researchers developing and optimizing AMPs. As a result, numerous AMP databases have emerged. The Antimicrobial Peptide Database (APD) is one of the most renowned AMP databases, first launched in 2003 and now evolved into APD3, containing 2619 AMPs with extensive functional annotations and search capabilities (18). DRAMP is another popular database that, in its recent update, included stapled AMPs and expanded AMP toxicity property, encompassing 22,259 entries (19). DBAASP is another open-access AMP database that, in its latest update, comprises over 15,700 records, including over 14,500 monomers and nearly 400 homo- and hetero-multimers, providing detailed information on their amino acid sequences, chemical modifications, 3D structures, bioactivities and toxicities, along with a structure modeling pipeline (20). CAMPR4 is another comprehensive AMP database that, besides updating AMP sequence information, introduced independent prediction algorithms for natural and synthetic AMPs, featuring 24,243 AMP sequences with detailed information, including sequence information, source organisms, target organisms, minimum inhibitory and hemolytic concentrations (21). LAMP is another AMP database that offers cross-links with other AMP databases (22).
We first introduced dbAMP in 2018 and updated it in 2022, collecting natural and synthetic AMPs with detailed annotations, including sequence information, activity, physicochemical properties and structural information (23,24). Since its launch, many studies have utilized dbAMP data to develop predictive models or construct databases (25–30). Considering the research community’s usage, in this update, we have collected 35,518 entries from over 5200 publications to further enrich the content of dbAMP. The highlights of the new version are illustrated in Figure 1. In addition to the expansion in the number of sequences, the new version of dbAMP integrates the tertiary structures of over 30,000 sequences, freely available for download. Furthermore, this version of dbAMP incorporates over 100 AMP-target protein docked complexes to assist researchers in exploring AMP mechanisms at the molecular level. The hemolytic toxicity and stability of AMPs are critical factors in determining their potential as clinical drugs. In this version, we integrate a computational framework that can effectively predict the hemolytic toxicity and half-life of AMPs. Additionally, we develop an AMP design platform, allowing users to design highly active, low-toxicity and stable AMPs. These updates make dbAMP an invaluable resource in the post-pandemic era and an indispensable platform for AMP research and design.
Highlighted improvements in dbAMP 3.0. dbAMP is the most comprehensive resource for AMPs with this update bringing the total values for the AMP sequences and curated articles to >35,000 and >5200, respectively.
material and methods:
In the post-pandemic era, the global issue of antibiotic resistance has become increasingly severe, accompanied by a sharp rise in the number of both natural and synthetic AMPs. This version of the dbAMP continues to utilize the terminology from the previous version, categorizing sequences with fewer than 100 amino acids as AMPs, while sequences longer than 100 amino acids are classified as antimicrobial proteins. We retrieved peer-reviewed literature from PubMed, Google Scholar and Web of Science by searching specific keywords such as ‘antimicrobial peptides’, ‘antibacterial peptides’, ‘antifungal peptides’, ‘antiviral peptides’, ‘antitumor peptides’ and ‘anticancer peptides’. The retrieved literature was subjected to manual reading and analysis, augmented by GPT-4 to expedite knowledge mining, from which AMP data were extracted. To prevent potential large language model ‘hallucinations’ from affecting database accuracy, we implemented strict quality control measures, including thorough manual review and cross-validation with multiple sources. Additionally, we retained the text mining system from dbAMP 2.0, enhancing the automatic identification of AMP-related articles through a scoring system. In this current version of the database, AMP data are collected from over 5200 articles. Furthermore, we integrated data from the UniProt database (31) and the Protein Data Bank (PDB) (32) to enrich the functional activity information of AMPs and provide experimentally validated 3D structural annotation.
Due to the challenges associated with the experimental determination of peptide and protein structures, most peptides lack experimentally determined structures (33,34). In this study, we employed ESMFold_V1 (ESMFold) to predict the potential 3D structures of AMP (35,36). ESMfold is an end-to-end structure prediction tool based on a protein language model that can directly generate high-resolution 3D structures from protein sequences. ESMfold utilizes the default structure prediction parameters: peptides are modeled as monomers, and multiple structural models are generated. For each peptide, ESMfold generated multiple structures (typically 5), and the structure with the highest predicted local distance difference test score was selected as the final predicted structure (37,38).

A contact map is a two-dimensional matrix that depicts the interactions between residues within a protein or peptide (43,44). It encodes the spatial proximity of residue pairs: when the Euclidean distance between the Cα atoms of two residues falls below a threshold (typically 8 Å), they are considered to be in ‘contact’. This interaction is represented as a matrix element. Contact maps are crucial for predicting and reconstructing the three-dimensional (3D) structures of proteins and peptides, especially in folding algorithms.
To construct a contact map, PDB files are parsed to extract the 3D coordinates of each residue, typically focusing on the Cα or Cβ atoms. The Euclidean distance between each pair of residues is calculated, and those with distances below the defined threshold (e.g., 8 Å) are marked as ‘contacts’. The resulting two-dimensional matrix visually represents the spatial interactions within the protein or peptide chain, providing a critical foundation for structure prediction and folding studies (45,46).
Protein secondary structure plays a critical role in understanding the 3D conformation and function of proteins. Accurate analysis of secondary structure is essential for elucidating the mechanisms by which proteins operate within cellular environments, thereby providing vital insights for drug design and functional prediction (47,48). We derive the secondary structure of AMP using the DSSP algorithm (Definition of Secondary Structure of Proteins). DSSP is a classical tool widely used to assign secondary structure to protein residues based on atomic-resolution PDB structures (49).
The DSSP algorithm begins by identifying hydrogen bonds within the protein backbone using an electrostatic definition. Specifically, DSSP assumes partial charges of −0.42 e on the carbonyl oxygen and +0.20 e on the amide hydrogen, with opposite charges assigned to the carbonyl carbon and amide nitrogen. A hydrogen bond is identified if the energy E calculated by the following equation is less than −0.5 kcal/mol:
where q1 = −0.42 e and q2 = +0.20 e are the partial charges on the carbonyl oxygen and amide hydrogen, respectively, and q3 = +0.42 e and q4 = −0.20 e are the partial charges on the carbonyl carbon and amide nitrogen, respectively. The terms rON, rCH, rOH and rCN represent the distances between the respective atoms: oxygen and nitrogen, carbon and hydrogen, oxygen and hydrogen and carbon and nitrogen.
Based on the identification of these hydrogen bonds, DSSP classifies protein residues into nine types of secondary structure: α-helix, 310-helix, π-helix, β-sheet, β-bridge, turn, high-curvature region, PPII helix and unclassified loop region. These secondary structure types are further grouped into three major classes: helices (including α-helix, 310-helix and π-helix), sheets (including β-sheet and β-bridge), and coils (including turns, high-curvature regions, PPII helices and loops). By applying DSSP, researchers can accurately derive secondary structure information from atomic-resolution PDB structures, providing a robust foundation for protein functional studies (50,51).
The home page provides a concise overview of dbAMP, highlighting key features and updates of the latest database version. This page also includes a quick search function. Additionally, this page offers news related to dbAMP and a video overview. From this page, users can access specific dbAMP pages, including Introduction, Browse, Search, Analyze, Tutorial and Download.
On the browse page, users can explore all AMPs and antimicrobial proteins stored in dbAMP. Additionally, this page provides filters that allow users to select the AMPs of interest based on functional activity, length, etc.
The search page offers three types of search functionalities: Basic Search, Structure Search and Advanced Search. Basic Search allows users to search using dbAMP ID and Sequence. Structure Search enables users to identify specific AMPs based on structure by utilizing Uniprot ID or PDB ID. Additionally, we provide a more precise Advanced Search option, which allows users to locate specific AMPs based on criteria such as length range, functional activity and source species.
Each entry in dbAMP includes an information page that provides detailed annotations on various aspects of the sequence. The specific content of the annotations may vary depending on the peptide. These annotations encompass basic information, an overview of protein modification sites, composition details, antimicrobial potency, physicochemical properties, interacting proteins, 3D structural annotations, docking information and more. Screenshots of the Search and Browse pages in dbAMP 3.0, as well as the general information page for AMPs.
The analyze page organizes the AMP analysis and prediction tools we developed:
AMPfinder, introduced in the previous version, is designed for genomic/metagenomic data mining for the discovery of AMPs.
AMPpredictor, also introduced in the previous version, utilizes machine learning methods to predict the functional activity of AMPs.
AVP-IFT(52) is a tool we developed for the identification and specific target characterization of antiviral peptides.
AMPActiPred(53) is a three-stage computational framework we developed for predicting antibacterial peptides and their activity levels based on a deep forest architecture.
HemoFinder, a new tool introduced in dbAMP 3.0, is used for predicting the hemolytic activity and half-life of AMPs.
A systematic pipeline, newly introduced in dbAMP 3.0, is designed for optimizing and designing AMPs with desirable clinical characteristics.
The tutorial page offers a concise guide to assist users in effectively navigating and utilizing dbAMP 3.0.
This page provides statistical information on different aspects of AMPs in this database, including statistics on functional activity, source species, amino acid composition and physicochemical properties of the AMPs.
The download page allows users to access and download all entries in dbAMP 3.0. To facilitate ease of use, we have categorized the entries based on AMP functional activity and source species, enabling more convenient and targeted downloads.
In the current version of dbAMP, data are stored in a MariaDB database (version 15.1) hosted on a LAMP server (Linux/Apache/MariaDB/PHP) running CentOS Linux 7.9.2009. The dbAMP website employs PHP (version 7.4.33) as the backend language. The frontend is constructed using HTML5, with CSS and the Bootstrap framework (version 3.4.1, https://getbootstrap.com/) applied for styling and layout. Interactivity is facilitated through JavaScript and the jQuery library (version 3.6.0, https://jquery.com/). The backend connects to the MariaDB database to query data, which is then served to the frontend for user display. We are responsible for the continuous updating and maintenance of dbAMP, including page optimization, bug fixes and incorporating user feedback and suggestions.

statistics page: This page provides statistical information on different aspects of AMPs in this database, including statistics on functional activity, source species, amino acid composition and physicochemical properties of the AMPs.
download page: The download page allows users to access and download all entries in dbAMP 3.0. To facilitate ease of use, we have categorized the entries based on AMP functional activity and source species, enabling more convenient and targeted downloads.
technical background: In the current version of dbAMP, data are stored in a MariaDB database (version 15.1) hosted on a LAMP server (Linux/Apache/MariaDB/PHP) running CentOS Linux 7.9.2009. The dbAMP website employs PHP (version 7.4.33) as the backend language. The frontend is constructed using HTML5, with CSS and the Bootstrap framework (version 3.4.1, https://getbootstrap.com/) applied for styling and layout. Interactivity is facilitated through JavaScript and the jQuery library (version 3.6.0, https://jquery.com/). The backend connects to the MariaDB database to query data, which is then served to the frontend for user display. We are responsible for the continuous updating and maintenance of dbAMP, including page optimization, bug fixes and incorporating user feedback and suggestions.
system overview and database updates:
The current version of dbAMP incorporates information extracted from over 5200 articles, significantly increasing the number of AMPs compared to dbAMP 2.0. As of June 2024, dbAMP includes 35,518 entries, comprising 33,065 AMPs and 2453 antimicrobial proteins, covering 6,227 target organisms and 18,408 AMP–target interactions. Table 1 outlines the improvements and updates in the current version of dbAMP. Based on literature and related database records, AMPs and antimicrobial proteins are functionally characterized within dbAMP, classified into eight major functional categories with a total of 58 functional activities, as detailed in Supplementary Table S1. The most prevalent category is antibacterial peptides (63.77%), followed by new functional peptides (14.47%), disease-associated peptides (8.26%), antifungal peptides (8.15%), antiviral peptides (3.15%), new mechanism-associated peptides (1.59%), toxic peptides (0.33%) and antiparasitic peptides (0.28%). The distribution of AMP source organisms is shown in Supplementary Figure S1.

In addition to the increase in entries, dbAMP 3.0 has also added over 30,000 tertiary structure annotations, from which peptide contact maps have been derived. Furthermore, to explore the molecular mechanisms of AMPs, dbAMP 3.0 integrates over 100 docked complexes utilizing docking technology. Additionally, in this version of AMP, we have developed HemoFinder, a tool for predicting AMP hemolytic activity and half-life, to help users identify AMPs with better drug-like potential. We also developed an efficient AMP design pipeline for developing AMPs with high antibacterial activity, low hemolytic toxicity, and high stability. Furthermore, we integrated our previously developed machine learning-based antibacterial peptide prediction tool, AMPActiPred, which effectively predicts ABPs, characterizes their activity against ten specific bacterial species, and quantitatively estimates their activity levels (53). Additionally, we included our previously published tool AVP-IFT for identifying antiviral peptides and characterizing their specific targets (52). Lastly, we have compiled over 20 existing and reliable AMP prediction tools and benchmark datasets, providing cross-linking to these resources to assist users in finding suitable tools to advance their modeling efforts. These tools can be found on the ‘Analyze’ page.
To evaluate the reliability of ESMFold in predicting AMP structures, we selected 100 peptides with experimentally determined structures and predicted their structures using ESMFold. The study employed two metrics, RMSD and TM-score, to assess the accuracy of the predictions, with the results summarized in Supplementary Table S2. The average RMSD between the experimentally determined PDB structures and the ESMFold predictions for these 100 peptides was 1.692 Å, which typically indicates high structural similarity since an RMSD below 2 Å is considered to reflect a high degree of concordance between the predicted and experimental structures. The majority of our predictions achieved RMSD values below 2 Å, demonstrating that ESMFold is capable of accurately modeling AMP structures. In terms of TM-score, which is a metric to evaluate the global structural similarity with a score above 0.5 reflecting similar overall folding patterns, the average TM-score was 0.704, further supporting the high accuracy of ESMFold in capturing the correct fold of AMP structures.
To further highlight the advantages of using ESMFold, we compared its performance against AlphaFold2 on the same set of 100 experimentally determined AMP structures and also measured the prediction time for each sequence. ESMFold achieved a lower average RMSD (1.692 Å) compared to AlphaFold2 (2.391 Å), indicating that ESMFold’s predicted structures are closer to the experimental references. Moreover, ESMFold yielded a higher average TM-score of 0.704 compared to AlphaFold2’s 0.6503, demonstrating its superior accuracy on short peptide sequences. In addition, ESMFold’s average prediction time was 1.33 s per sequence, whereas AlphaFold2 required 54.38 s on average, making ESMFold approximately 50 times faster. This significant speed advantage is crucial for handling large-scale peptide datasets, such as the 35,000+ sequences in our dbAMP database.

To explore the molecular mechanisms of AMPs, dbAMP utilizes docking technology, integrating over 100 docked complexes. Previous studies indicate AMPs frequently interact with lipopolysaccharides (LPS) of Gram-negative bacteria (55). In dbAMP 3.0, AMPs with fewer than 15 amino acids and known activity against Gram-negative bacteria were selected as ligands. The modified LptB2FG protein (PDB: 6MI7), involved in LPS transport in Gram-negative bacteria, was chosen as the target protein (56,57).
The docking simulations were performed using the ezPPDock function on the ezCADD server (58). This process involves several key steps: first, preparing and importing the structures of the receptor (LptB2FG) and ligand (AMP); then, employing a scoring function that integrates shape complementarity, electrostatic interactions, and desolvation free energy; and finally, using a Katchalski–Katzir algorithm with Fast Fourier Transform for rigid-body docking. The top poses were selected based on the strength of their interactions around the LPS binding site.
Then dbAMP visually depicts the interactions between AMPs and the LptB2FG protein-LPS complex, aiding researchers in understanding AMP mechanisms. Figure 4 illustrates the docked complexes and 2D-interaction diagrams generated using LigPlus within dbAMP (59). Notably, this method employs a scoring system rather than binding energy to represent results, with higher scores indicating stronger interactions.

The insights gained from these molecular docking studies can significantly contribute to the development and modification of peptides. By identifying key interaction sites and favorable structural features, researchers can design AMPs with enhanced binding affinity to target proteins like LptB2FG. This approach allows for the rational optimization of peptide sequences, potentially leading to more effective AMPs with improved specificity.
AMPs defend against pathogens by disrupting microbial cell membranes. Many AMPs are positively charged and interact with the negatively charged bacterial cell membranes, which is a common mechanism of action. However, this raises concerns about their toxicity to mammalian cells. Many AMPs have hemolytic activity, which can damage the red blood cell membranes of mammalian cells and release hemoglobin. Therefore, hemolytic activity is an important clinical feature to consider when converting AMPs into potential drugs. While traditional wet lab methods can effectively assess hemolytic activity, they require substantial resources. In the latest version of dbAMP, we developed HemoFinder, a machine-learning scheme that effectively predicts AMP hemolytic activity. The workflow of HemoFinder is shown in Supplementary Figure S2. We used a dataset from previous studies, which includes 1359 high-hemolytic peptides and 1,198 low-hemolytic peptides (60). The sizes of the train and test sets are shown in Supplementary Table S3. HemoFinder employs five common peptide descriptors, including AAC, DPC, PAAC, CKSAAGP and PHYC, which effectively characterize the peptide’s composition and physicochemical properties. HemoFinder uses common machine learning algorithms, including XGBoost, Decision Tree, KNN and Random Forest as base learners, and a soft voting strategy to build the final classifier to identify high-hemolysis peptides. Table 2 presents the performance of HemoFinder in predicting hemolytic activity. Evidently, HemoFinder achieves state-of-the-art performance compared to other methods, with an accuracy of 81.67% and an MCC of 0.6336, demonstrating balanced predictions. In summary, HemoFinder, integrated into the dbAMP 3.0, effectively aids researchers in predicting the hemolytic toxicity of AMPs, thereby facilitating the design of low-toxicity AMPs.

The latest version of dbAMP integrated a systematic pipeline for optimizing an input peptide sequence to generate AMPs with desirable clinical characteristics. Ideally, an AMP should exhibit high antimicrobial activity, low hemolytic activity, and a long half-life. Our AMP design pipeline utilized PyAMPA (62) as the template for its genetic algorithm for optimization. Building upon this template, we incorporated our own models for predicting characteristics such as antimicrobial activity and hemolytic activity of a peptide (Figure 5A). Specifically, hemolytic activity and half-life are calculated using the HemoFinder module, while antimicrobial activity is assessed using our previously published tool, AMPActiPred (53). These models replaced the original models in PyAMPA to provide more reliable predictions. In addition to the three peptide characteristics, our pipeline considered a fourth attribute of AMPs: quantitative antibacterial activity level prediction, i.e. the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) prediction, which is also assessed by AMPActiPred. AMPActiPred not only predicts whether a peptide is an AMP but also quantitatively forecasts MICs of AMPs against ten bacterial species. Here, the AMPActiPred’s output is log MIC, representing the activity level of the AMPs, with the unit in μM. Its performance is summarized in Supplementary Table S4 and illustrated in Supplementary Figure S4. By incorporating the MIC predictions into the pipeline, users can customize their AMPs to target different types of bacteria. Initially, the pipeline generates 100 sequences through random mutations, which constitute the first generation of peptides. Twenty percent of the peptides with the highest fitness scores are selected to replace the initial population. These peptides then undergo single-point crossings and single-point mutations to generate new sequences. The new sequences are subsequently assessed for the aforementioned key clinical characteristics, and their fitness scores are calculated. By default, the pipeline operates for 100 iterations or terminates iteration if no improvement in fitness scores is observed after 20 rounds. The sequence with the highest fitness score is then selected, and its helical wheel projections are visualized to allow users to compare the differences between the initial and optimized sequences.
Figure 6 illustrates an example of sequence optimization by the pipeline introduced by dbAMP. The initial sequence exhibited low antimicrobial activity and significant hemolytic toxicity, making it unsuitable for clinical use. Additionally, the original sequence had a low half-life, potentially reducing its druggability (Figure 6A). Starting from the initial sequence, we employs a carefully designed genetic algorithm with a fitness function, iteratively balancing antimicrobial activity, hemolytic activity, and half-life to generate peptides with favorable clinical characteristics (Figure 6B). We used ESMFold to evaluate the tertiary structures of the original sequence and the optimized sequence, as shown in Figure 6A. The sequences generated in each iteration and their clinical properties are shown in Supplementary Table S5. To further validate the optimization process, we conducted docking studies with proteins surrounding LPS, using the ezPPDock function on the ezCADD server, demonstrated that the optimized peptide achieved better docking results and improved scores. The two-dimensional protein-protein interaction analysis, conducted using LigPlus software and illustrated in Supplementary Figure S6, revealed that substitutions T12F, L11R and L9Y of the optimized peptide created more hydrogen bonds, further confirming that this pipeline effectively designs sequences with enhanced antimicrobial potential. The docking score improved from 3071.16 for the original peptide to 3549.94 for the optimized peptide, indicating enhanced potential for LPS interaction. For comparison, we included Thanatin, a well-characterized AMP with strong LPS-binding properties, which achieved a docking score of 3761.54 (63). This analysis suggests that our optimized peptide has developed interactions with LPS and surrounding residues comparable to those of mature AMPs, supporting the effectiveness of our database-driven optimization pipeline. We developed a user-friendly web interface for this pipeline (Supplementary Figure S7), where users can specify parameters to adjust the fitness function and prioritize different clinical characteristics according to their specific goals. To further provide experimental validation evidence for HemoFinder and this optimization pipeline, we conducted a case study, the results of which are shown in the supplementary materials. The results of the case study indicate that the predictions derived from our developed methods are consistent with the experimental findings, thereby further validating the efficacy of the tools incorporated within dbAMP.

In recent years, with the growth of data and the optimization of algorithms, many tools have been developed to predict AMPs. The various methods are entirely distinct, which can appear confusing at first glance. Therefore, dbAMP 3.0 has conducted a comprehensive survey of existing computational methods and developed a web page for prediction tools, gathering over 20 novel and reliable AMP prediction tools. Additionally, dbAMP 3.0 has collected more than 20 commonly used benchmark datasets related to AMP prediction tasks. We believe that dbAMP 3.0 can serve as an efficient platform to help researchers quickly and easily compare classification methods, select appropriate tools and download relevant datasets, thus advancing the modeling process.

portal of amp prediction tools and bench: In recent years, with the growth of data and the optimization of algorithms, many tools have been developed to predict AMPs. The various methods are entirely distinct, which can appear confusing at first glance. Therefore, dbAMP 3.0 has conducted a comprehensive survey of existing computational methods and developed a web page for prediction tools, gathering over 20 novel and reliable AMP prediction tools. Additionally, dbAMP 3.0 has collected more than 20 commonly used benchmark datasets related to AMP prediction tasks. We believe that dbAMP 3.0 can serve as an efficient platform to help researchers quickly and easily compare classification methods, select appropriate tools and download relevant datasets, thus advancing the modeling process.
conclusion:
AMR has emerged as a global public health threat, and its significance has been further amplified in the post-pandemic era. Among the potential alternatives to traditional antibiotics, AMPs have garnered considerable attention. The dbAMP is a renowned repository focused on AMPs, including both natural and synthetic AMPs. It offers comprehensive annotations, covering sequence information, functional activity information and physicochemical properties. Compared to the previous version, the highlights of this update are as follows:
Comprehensive update on AMP data: This update incorporates 33,065 AMPs and 2453 antimicrobial proteins, collected from over 5200 research articles. This represents an increase of more than 6800 AMPs and antimicrobial proteins compared to the previous version.
Extensive annotation of AMP tertiary structures: The current version of dbAMP utilizes ESMFold to predict the tertiary structures of over 30,000 previously unannotated AMPs, providing valuable structural information for clinical drug development. Additionally, dbAMP 3.0 includes calculated contact maps and corresponding secondary structures based on these tertiary structures, which are available for free download.
Integration of AMP-protein interactions with docking: dbAMP integrates over 100 docking complexes using molecular docking techniques to help scientists explore the mechanisms of AMP action.
Tools for predicting AMP hemolytic toxicity and half-life: The hemolytic toxicity and stability of AMPs are critical factors in determining their potential as clinical drugs. In this update, we have developed HemoFinder, a tool capable of effectively predicting the hemolytic toxicity and half-life of AMPs.
A systematic pipeline for designing AMPs with favorable clinical characteristics: The dbAMP integrates a systematic pipeline, which aids researchers in designing high-activity, low-toxicity and highly stable AMPs based on template peptides.
Collection and cross-linking to current reliable AMP prediction tools: In recent years, numerous tools have been developed to predict AMPs due to the growth of data and advancements in algorithms. The latest version of dbAMP provides a comprehensive survey of existing tools and has developed a continuously updated web page that includes over 20 reliable AMP prediction tools and their cross-linkings. Additionally, more than 20 AMP-related benchmark datasets have been incorporated to help users select the appropriate datasets and tools through our interface.
We believe that this new version of dbAMP will become an invaluable resource in the AMP field and an indispensable platform for researchers analyzing and developing novel AMPs.
